titleEn: I rejoiced when they said to me
progression: | G D | Em C | G D | G G |
intro: One of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, and the one that describes arriving. The speaker is quoted secondhand in verse 1, standing inside the gates by verse 2, and from verse 6 he stops describing the city and starts talking to it. That turn is the grammar lesson: from verse 6 to the end almost every line carries a second person feminine singular suffix, your gates, those who love you, your walls, your palaces, within you, for you, because the addressee is a city and cities are feminine in Hebrew. In many Ashkenazi communities the Songs of Ascents are said after Minchah on the Shabbatot between Sukkot and Passover.

stichs.en: A song of ascents. Of David.
I rejoiced when they said to me: let us go to the house of the LORD.

verses.summary: The joy is dated to the invitation, not to the arrival. What the speaker reports is the moment other people included him in their plural verb, let us go.
A participle plus the verb to be, which in Hebrew stretches an action out in time: not we arrived but we have been standing there. The pronoun has already turned from I to our.

stichs.en: like a city knit together with itself.

verses.summary: The first thing said about the city is architectural: it is dense, its buildings touch, there are no gaps. The verse offers that as a description of a people as much as of masonry.

stichs.en: There the tribes went up, the tribes of the LORD,
a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.

verses.summary: The compactness of verse 3 gets its explanation: this is where separate tribes converged. The word for going up is the same root as the ascents in the heading.

stichs.en: For there thrones were set for judgment,
thrones of the house of David.

verses.summary: The second reason to come up, next to worship: this is where cases were heard. The verb is the ordinary one for sitting, with thrones as its subject, so the furniture is what sits.

stichs.en: Ask after the peace of Jerusalem;
may those who love you be at ease.

verses.summary: The pivot of the psalm. Description stops, instruction starts, and in the second half the city is addressed directly for the first time as you.

stichs.en: Let there be peace within your walls,

verses.summary: Two zones named in order, the defensive wall and the buildings behind it, and a different word for calm in each. The outer one asks for peace, the inner one for quiet.

stichs.en: For the sake of my brothers and my friends,
let me say: peace be within you.

verses.summary: The reason given for blessing the city is other people. The speaker wants nothing from Jerusalem for himself and says so before he says the blessing.

stichs.en: For the sake of the house of the LORD our God,
let me seek good for you.

verses.summary: The second reason, matching the first phrase of verse 8 word for word, and the psalm closes where verse 1 pointed: at the house. Seeking good is an action, not a wish.

pardes.body: Nine verses in two halves. Verses 1 to 5 look at Jerusalem and report: an invitation, feet in the gates, a compact city, tribes coming up, thrones for judgment. Verses 6 to 9 turn and speak to it. The two halves are joined by what the city is for, which the psalm gives twice, once as worship in verse 4 and once as justice in verse 5, and then repeats in reverse at the end, friends in verse 8 and the house in verse 9. Notice that {{2.0}} and {{2.1}} are a participle plus a past tense verb, a construction that holds an action open in time, so the standing is not a snapshot.

Verse 6 is built on one consonant cluster repeated four times: {{6.0}} ask, {{6.1}} the peace of, {{6.2}} Jerusalem, {{6.3}} may they be at ease. The name of the city carries the sound of peace inside it, and the verse makes that audible rather than arguing it. Two words are commonly mistranslated. {{7.2}} is a rampart, the outer defensive work, not wealth, though the two are spelled alike. {{3.3}} is a passive of the verb to join, so the city is joined to itself, which older translations render compact. The name in {{2.4}} is written short in the consonants and pointed as a dual by the Masoretes, and what the ending means, two cities or an old locative form, is disputed.

The two institutions of verses 4 and 5, the pilgrimage and the court, are what made the city a destination, and later readers took the pairing as a claim that worship without justice has no address. The joining of verse 3 attracted a long line of reading in which the city below is matched by a city above and the two are fastened to each other, so that praying for Jerusalem's peace is not local politics. That reading is repeated widely in later literature and is not stated in the verse itself. The instruction in verse 6 is one of the few in the book that tells you what to say rather than what to feel, and it has been treated as an obligation on anyone who benefits from the place, which is the logic verse 8 spells out.

In the mystical reading the city is a receiver, which is why the whole second half addresses it in the feminine and asks that it be filled rather than that it act. Verse 7 names two vessels in order, the rampart and the palaces, and asks for a different quality in each, peace at the boundary and stillness inside, which is the standard shape of a container being prepared. The joining of {{3.3}} is read as the seam between what is above and what is below, and the ascents of the heading as the fifteen steps of that climb. The last word of the psalm is for you, so the whole movement ends by handing everything it gathered back to the place it came for.
